questions.question: A catalog administrator is adding a docking station to the catalog. Employees order the docking station by itself, but its power cable only makes sense together with the dock. How should these be modeled?

options.text: Make both the docking station and the cable separate catalog items
Make the docking station a catalog item and the cable part of it
Make the cable a catalog item and the docking station a content item
Make both of them content items within a single order guide

explanation.correct: The docs define a catalog item as a good or service that can be ordered by itself; something that only makes sense as part of a greater whole belongs to an item rather than being an item on its own. The dock is ordered on its own, so it is the catalog item, and the cable is part of it. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_IntroductionToCatalogItems.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The cable only makes sense with the dock, so per the docs it is part of an item, not a stand-alone catalog item that users order by itself.
Content items provide information instead of goods or services, so the orderable dock cannot be one, and the cable is not orderable on its own.
Order guides group multiple catalog items in one request, and content items only provide information, so neither fits an orderable dock and its cable.

source.excerpt: A catalog item is anything that can be ordered on its own, like a laptop, while components like a CPU are not.

questions.question: Customers ordering a PC from the catalog must be able to choose extra memory, and the price should change based on their choice. What should the catalog administrator add to the PC catalog item?

options.text: A content item describing the memory options
A variable that captures the memory choice
A record producer for memory upgrades
A separate catalog item for each memory size

explanation.correct: Service catalog variables capture the choices a customer makes when ordering an item and shape the item form. The docs use this exact example: a Memory variable offering memory options at extra cost for a PC item, and variables can be defined to affect the item price. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_ServiceCatalogVariables.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A content item provides information instead of goods or services; it cannot capture the customer's memory choice or adjust the price of the PC.
A record producer creates task-based records such as incidents from the catalog; it is not used to collect ordering options on a PC item.
Extra memory only makes sense as part of the PC, so per the docs it belongs to that item rather than being a separate orderable catalog item.

source.excerpt: Service Catalog variables are global and customize items to customer needs, like offering different operating systems for computers.

questions.question: A catalog administrator maintains 10 server catalog items that all ask the same five questions. A sixth question must now appear on all 10 items. What setup lets future changes like this be made only once?

options.text: Add the new question to each item one by one
Move the shared questions into a variable set
Group the 10 server items together in an order guide
Convert the 10 server items into a record producer

explanation.correct: Variable sets are reusable collections of variables that can be attached to multiple catalog items and order guides. The docs use this server example: associating the same variables item by item is repetitive and error-prone, whereas a change made to the set is reflected in every item that uses it. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_ServiceCatalogVariableSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Adding the question to each item individually is the repetitive, error-prone approach the docs describe; every later change would again need 10 edits.
An order guide submits one request that generates several items; it does not share variable definitions across the forms of separate catalog items.
A record producer creates task-based records such as incidents instead of requested items, so it is not a way to share questions across server items.

source.excerpt: Instead of adding variables to each item separately, Variable Sets group them, saving time and reducing errors. Updates to a Variable Set apply to all associated items.

questions.question: Employees find the standard incident form confusing, so the service desk team wants them to report issues from the service catalog through a simpler, catalog-style form that still creates incident records. What should the administrator build?

options.text: A new order guide
A record producer
A new content item
A standard catalog item

explanation.correct: A record producer is a type of catalog item that lets end users create task-based records, such as incidents, from the service catalog. The docs recommend it as a better end-user experience than the regular task form: it looks like a catalog item but generates a task record instead of a requested item. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_RecordProducer.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: An order guide submits a single catalog request that generates several catalog items; it does not create an incident record from a simple form.
Content items provide information instead of goods or services, so submitting one would not create an incident record for the service desk.
A standard catalog item is ordered through a request and requested item; the docs note a record producer is what generates a task record like an incident.

source.excerpt: A Record Producer in ServiceNow is a catalog item that lets users create task-based records, like incidents, more easily than using a standard form.

questions.question: When a new employee is hired, the manager should submit one catalog request that orders business cards, a computer, and a cell phone based on the employee's location and job title. What should the catalog administrator create?

options.text: A record producer
An order guide
A variable set
A content item

explanation.correct: An order guide submits a single service catalog request that generates several items. The docs give a New Employee Hire guide as the example: the customer enters details such as location and job title, rule conditions decide which items to order, and cascading variables pass common information to those items. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_ServiceCatalogOrderGuides.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A record producer creates a task-based record such as an incident from the catalog; it does not order several catalog items in one request.
A variable set is a reusable group of variables attached to items; it collects answers but does not order multiple catalog items together.
Content items provide information instead of goods or services, so one cannot order business cards, a computer, and a phone for the new hire.

source.excerpt: Order Guides let users request multiple related items at once and help them decide what they need, with variables arranged by order number.

questions.question: A catalog administrator wants Facilities owners to create and maintain their own catalog items through a guided, visual experience, limited to approved catalogs, categories, and variable types. Which approach fits?

options.text: Order guides with cascading variables
Catalog Builder with item templates
Variable sets with catalog UI policies
Workflow Studio with fulfillment flows

explanation.correct: Catalog Builder provides a visual, guided experience for creating and editing catalog items and record producers, so catalog maintenance can be delegated. Administrators create templates that pre-set values and restrict catalogs, categories, variable types, and portal settings for items built from them. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/catalog-builder.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Order guides submit one request that generates several items and pass shared answers through cascading variables; they are not an authoring tool for items.
Variable sets group reusable variables for items; they do not give business owners a guided, restricted way to create and maintain catalog items.
Workflow Studio flows define fulfillment processes such as approvals and tasks after an item is ordered; they do not author the catalog items themselves.

source.excerpt: Create or edit catalog items and record producers visually with guidelines and restrictions using the Catalog Builder.

questions.question: A knowledge manager creates a knowledge base but adds no Can Read or Can Contribute user criteria. The glide.knowman.block_access_with_no_user_criteria property is still at its default value. Who can read the articles?

options.text: Any user, including unauthenticated users
Knowledge admins and the base owner or manager
Any user who has at least one role assigned
Any user who has the snc_internal role assigned

explanation.correct: When no read criteria apply, the docs say access depends on glide.knowman.block_access_with_no_user_criteria, whose default value is true. With true, no one can read except users with special knowledge privileges (knowledge admins and the base's owner and manager) and users with contribute access, which no one else has here. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/user-access-knowledge.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Every user, including unauthenticated users, gets read access only when the property is set to false; at its default of true, access is blocked.
Users with at least one role can contribute only when the property is false; at the default of true, regular users get neither contribute nor read access.
The snc_internal Can Read criterion is added automatically only when the Explicit Roles plugin is active; here no Can Read criteria exist, so at the default of true regular users get no read access.

source.excerpt: If there is no user criteria on the can read related list, then the knowledge base becomes open to the public.

questions.question: An employee finds that a knowledge article has outdated steps and wants to send suggested corrections to the knowledge team without the suggestion appearing on the article page. What should the employee do?

options.text: Give the article a one-star rating
Click Flag Article and enter the changes
Answer No to the Helpful? question
Post a comment at the bottom of the article

explanation.correct: Flag Article is the feedback option for incorrect or inappropriate content: clicking it opens a window where the user enters suggested changes. Flagged comments do not appear on the Article View page; knowledge managers and admins review them under Knowledge > Articles > All Flagged. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/r_KnowledgeFeedback.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The star rating only indicates the article's effectiveness on a scale of 1 to 5; it gives the user no place to enter suggested changes.
The Helpful? question only takes a simple Yes or No answer about the article's usefulness, so it cannot carry the suggested corrections.
Article comments use Live Feed and users can view comments directly on the article, so a comment would appear on the article page.

source.excerpt: Users can also provide feedback by commenting or flagging articles, which notifies kb administrators.

questions.question: A service desk manager wants employees to get immediate help with common IT issues through a chat interface in channels such as Slack or Microsoft Teams, so technicians handle fewer simple incidents. Which ServiceNow application fits this need?

options.text: Catalog Builder
Virtual Agent
Workflow Studio
Branding Editor

explanation.correct: Virtual Agent lets employees and customers serve themselves through a messaging interface with prebuilt conversations powered by AI, and it can escalate to a human. ITSM Virtual Agent deflects the most common, simpler incidents and can be offered on familiar channels such as Slack and Microsoft Teams. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/conversational-interfaces/virtual-agent/virtual-agent-landing-page.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Catalog Builder is a guided experience for creating and editing catalog items and record producers so catalog maintenance can be delegated; it is not a chat interface for employees.
Workflow Studio is where flows, subflows, and actions are built to automate multi-step processes; it does not give employees a chat interface.
Branding Editor gives a Service Portal portal its own look and feel (theme colors, logo, and similar settings); it does not provide conversations.

source.excerpt: Virtual Agent provides an intelligent chat experience, answering common questions and resolving routine issues using AI and natural language.

questions.question: A knowledge manager adds a user criteria record for the Support department to the Can Contribute related list of a knowledge base. Which two things can Support users now do in that knowledge base? (Choose two)

options.text: Read the articles in the knowledge base
Create new user criteria records
Create, modify, and retire articles
Add user criteria to the base's related lists

explanation.correct: Per the docs, Can Contribute users "can create, modify, and retire knowledge articles in a knowledge base", and "contribute access to a knowledge base also provides read access to all articles in the knowledge base." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/t_SelectUserCriteria.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Creating a new user criteria record (clicking New) is done by a user with the admin role, and from the Knowledge module requires the user_criteria_admin role; contribute access does not grant it.
Adding existing user criteria to a knowledge base's related lists requires the knowledge_manager, knowledge_admin, or admin role, not contribute access.

source.excerpt: User criteria include can read, can't read; can contribute, can't contribute.

questions.question: A user submits one catalog request containing a laptop and a desk. The laptop's flow creates imaging and delivery tasks, while the desk's flow creates only a delivery task. Where are these catalog tasks attached?

options.text: They attach directly to the parent request
Each one belongs to the requested item it fulfills
They attach to the catalog item definition records
One shared task covers both of the requested items

explanation.correct: Each catalog item in a request creates its own discrete requested item. The Create Catalog Task action creates a Catalog Task [sc_task] record associated with a requested item [sc_req_item], the item the task fulfills, so the laptop's tasks sit under its requested item and the desk's under its own. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/create-catalog-task-flow-designer.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Create Catalog Task action links each task to a requested item record, not directly to the parent request that groups the items together.
Catalog item definitions describe what can be ordered; tasks are created at fulfillment time and associated with a specific requested item record.
Each catalog item in the request produces its own requested item, and each task references the single requested item it fulfills, so tasks are not shared.

source.excerpt: In a Service Catalog, a request can include multiple items, and each item can have several tasks... Even if tasks have similar names, they are specific to each item, because the steps for each may vary.

questions.question: An employee working in the ServiceNow AI Platform UI instead of a portal wants one list of the requests and incidents they have submitted. Which module should they open?

options.text: Self-Service > My Requests
Catalog Administration > My Request Filter
Feedback Management > My Flagged
Catalog Definition > User Criteria

explanation.correct: The docs describe filtering "incidents, requests, or tasks under the Self-Service > My Requests module in ServiceNow AI Platform", the same list the My Requests widget shows in Service Portal. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/configure-my-requests.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Service Catalog > Catalog Administration > My Request Filter is where a catalog_admin or admin defines the filters that My Requests uses; it is not where requesters view their own records.
Knowledge > Feedback Management > My Flagged lists the knowledge articles a user with the knowledge role has flagged, not their requests.
Service Catalog > Catalog Definition > User Criteria is where user criteria records are created to control access to catalog items and categories.

source.excerpt: After submitting a request, users can track it through All, Self-Service, My Requests.

questions.question: While editing an article in the IT knowledge base, a contributor needs a Printers subcategory under Hardware that does not exist yet. Category editing is enabled for that knowledge base. What can the contributor do?

options.text: Request new Can Contribute user criteria
Add it from the Category picker while editing
Flag the article so a manager adds the category
Create a separate knowledge base named Printers

explanation.correct: Each knowledge base has a hierarchy of categories that organizes its articles and helps users find them. When editing an article, a contributor can select categories with the Category picker and "add or edit categories if enabled for the knowledge base" by clicking the add category icon (+). See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/t_SelectACategory.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Can Contribute user criteria control who can create, modify, and retire articles; this contributor already has that access, and user criteria do not create categories.
Flag Article is for reporting incorrect or inappropriate content with suggested changes; it is not how categories are added.
Categories are created within a knowledge base as parent-child hierarchies; a new knowledge base would not place Printers under Hardware in the IT base.

source.excerpt: Categories help organize knowledge bases and make articles easier to find.

questions.question: A portal team has two tasks: a business analyst with no coding skills must give the company portal its own look and feel, and an expert developer must write scripts to power a custom widget. Which two Service Portal tools fit these tasks? (Choose two)

options.text: Branding Editor
Workflow Studio
Widget Editor
Decision tables

explanation.correct: Per the Service Portal overview, "Less technical users can make basic configuration changes to the UI using Branding Editor", which is used "to give your portal its own look and feel", while "Expert users can use the Widget Editor tool to write scripts to power a portal." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-user-interface/service-portal/c_ServicePortal.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Workflow Studio is used to build flows, subflows, and actions that automate processes, not to brand a portal or script widgets.
Workflow Studio decision tables separate decision logic from code by maintaining decision rules; they do not style portals or edit widgets.

source.excerpt: Service Portal allows users to search knowledge bases, browse catalogs, make requests, create and view incidents, and check system status.

questions.question: A user with the catalog editor role, assigned to the Laptop catalog item, wants to reuse the existing Shipping details variable set on that item and also create a new Accessories variable set. What can the catalog editor do?

options.text: Create both, since editors manage variable sets
Attach the existing set but not create the new one
Create the new set but not attach the existing one
Neither, since attaching sets needs an admin

explanation.correct: Variable sets are reusable collections of variables. The docs state that "catalog managers and catalog editors can attach a variable set for items to which they are assigned. However, catalog managers and catalog editors cannot create a variable set." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_ServiceCatalogVariableSets.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Catalog editors cannot create variable sets, so they cannot do both.
This reverses the rule: editors can attach existing sets to their assigned items but cannot create new sets.
Catalog managers and catalog editors can attach a variable set to items to which they are assigned, so attaching is not limited to admins.

questions.question: An administrator needs a new Justification variable to appear between the Requested for variable (Order 100) and the Laptop model variable (Order 200) on a catalog item form. What should the administrator do?

options.text: Set its Order value to 50
Set its Order value to 150
Set its Order value to 250
Create it after Laptop model

explanation.correct: The Order field on a variable sets where it is placed on the catalog item form: variables are arranged top to bottom from the lowest to the highest Order value. A value of 150 falls between 100 and 200, so Justification displays below Requested for and above Laptop model. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/t_CreateAVariableForACatalogItem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: An Order value of 50 is lower than 100, so the variable would appear above Requested for at the top of the form, not between the two variables.
An Order value of 250 is higher than 200, so the variable would appear below Laptop model rather than between Requested for and Laptop model.
Placement on the form is driven by the Order field value, not by when the variable was created, so creation sequence does not position it.

questions.question: A process analyst builds a flow with an Updated record trigger on the Incident table, and the flow includes an Ask for Approval action. Which run option should the trigger use?

options.text: For each unique change, even while running
Once, for the life of the record
Only if not currently running on the record
For every update, regardless of running flows

explanation.correct: Record triggers start a flow when a record is created or updated, and an Updated trigger requires choosing when to run the flow. The docs note that "Flows including approval actions should only run the trigger once", and Once "Triggers the flow once for the life of the record." To resubmit an approval, use Go back to flow logic instead. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/flow-triggers.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: For each unique change triggers the flow for every unique update, even while it is running, so the approval could be requested repeatedly; approval flows should run the trigger once.
Only if not currently running still triggers the flow for every unique record change whenever it is not already running, so it can start more than once.
For every update triggers the flow each time the record is updated regardless of running contexts, the opposite of running once.

questions.question: A process analyst adding steps to a Workflow Studio flow needs to use core actions rather than flow logic. Which two of these are Workflow Studio core actions? (Choose two)

options.text: Ask for Approval, to request approval on a record
For Each, to apply actions to each record in a list
Create Record, to create a record on any table
If, to run actions when its conditions are true

explanation.correct: The docs list both Ask for Approval ("Request approval for a record") and Create Record ("Creates a record on any table") as "Available as a Workflow Studio ServiceNow core action", which users with the flow_designer or admin role can add to a flow. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/ask-approval-flow-designer.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: For Each is flow logic: it applies one or more actions to each record in a list of records. It is not an action.
If is flow logic that runs the actions inside it only when its conditions evaluate to true. It is not an action.

questions.question: An administrator creates a user criteria record with Locations set to London and Companies set to Acme, leaving Match All at its default. A user based in Paris who works for Acme is evaluated. What is the result?

options.text: Matched, because one populated condition is met
Not matched, because both conditions must be met
Not matched until an Advanced script returns true
Not matched, because the Users field is empty

explanation.correct: Match All is cleared by default "so that any condition met provides a match". With it cleared, "the user must meet one or more of the set user criteria to be given access", so meeting the Acme company condition is enough. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/create-user-criteria-record-in-knowledge-management.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Requiring every condition applies only when Match All is selected; it is cleared by default.
The Script field is optional and only appears when Advanced is selected; it is not required for the location or company conditions to match.
With Match All cleared, meeting any populated condition gives a match; an empty Users field does not block the company match.

questions.question: When employees order a particular catalog item, an incident and a change request must be created automatically. How should a process analyst build this in Workflow Studio?

options.text: A flow with a Service Catalog trigger and Create Record actions
A flow with a Created trigger on the Incident table
A flow with an inbound email trigger and Create Record actions
A flow with a Daily scheduled trigger and Create Record actions

explanation.correct: The Service Catalog application trigger "Starts a flow from a Service Catalog item request", and the Create Record core action "Creates a record on any table", so one Create Record action can create the incident and another the change request. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/flow-triggers.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A Created trigger on Incident starts a flow only when an incident record is created, so it would not fire when the item is ordered.
Inbound email triggers start a flow when the instance receives an email, not when a catalog item is ordered.
A Daily scheduled trigger starts the flow at a set time every day, not when an employee orders the item.

questions.question: An administrator publishes a record producer named Report a broken printer that targets the Incident table. After an employee submits it from the service catalog, what record does it generate?

options.text: An incident record in the target table
A request containing one requested item
A requested item that links to an incident
A catalog task for the fulfillment group

explanation.correct: A record producer looks like a catalog item but generates a task-based record, such as an incident, instead of a requested item. The docs add that record producers should be used to create task-based records only, and that requested items should be created through regular catalog items so standard catalog processes run. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_RecordProducer.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: A request with requested items is what an ordinary catalog item produces; a record producer creates a record in its target table instead.
Record producers generate a task record such as an incident instead of a requested item, and the docs advise against creating requested items from them.
Catalog tasks are created for a requested item during request fulfillment; a record producer writes directly to its target table such as Incident.

questions.question: A developer is planning automation in Workflow Studio. Which two statements about flows, subflows, and triggers are true? (Choose two)

options.text: Subflows have no trigger and run when a flow or script calls them
Flows run in the foreground by default for immediate updates
Scheduled triggers use the instance timezone to decide start times
Service Catalog triggers can use catalog variables in their conditions

explanation.correct: The docs say that "In contrast to flows, subflows do not have a trigger but instead run when called from a playbook, flow, another subflow, or a script", and that "Scheduled triggers use the instance timezone to determine when to start a flow." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/exploring-subflows.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Run flow in background is the default: the flow runs asynchronously. Running in the foreground is an option for immediate updates, not the default.
The docs state that Service Catalog triggers do not support catalog variables as part of the trigger condition; get or create catalog variables in the body of the flow instead.

questions.question: An administrator needs catalog requests for items priced over $1,000 to get manager approval before fulfillment, while cheaper items need none. How should the approval be built in the item's Workflow Studio flow?

options.text: Use a trigger condition on a catalog price variable
Put Ask for Approval inside an If block on the price
Set the Ask for Approval rule to All users approve
Run two Ask for Approval actions in parallel branches

explanation.correct: If flow logic runs the actions inside it only when its conditions, built from record data, evaluate to true, and Ask for Approval requests approval for a record. Placing Ask for Approval inside an If block that checks the price asks for approval only on expensive requests. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/build-workflows/workflow-studio/flow-logic-if.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Service Catalog triggers do not support catalog variables as part of the trigger condition; the docs say to get catalog variables in the body of the flow.
Approval rules such as All users approve define which listed approvers must approve; they do not make the approval depend on price, so every request would still need approval.
The docs warn not to duplicate Ask for Approval actions in Do the following in parallel flow logic, and parallel branches add no price check.

questions.question: The HR and IT teams each want their own set of knowledge articles with their own managers, their own category structure, and separate control over who can read and contribute. What should the knowledge administrator set up?

options.text: A separate knowledge base for each team
One article template for each of the teams
One shared base with a category per team
A knowledge subscription for each team

explanation.correct: Knowledge Management supports multiple knowledge bases for different groups in an organization. Each knowledge base can be assigned its own managers, has its own category hierarchy, and gets its own read and contribute permissions through user criteria, so a base per team meets every requirement. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/knowledge-management/exploring-knowledge-management.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Article templates give knowledge articles a consistent structure; they do not assign separate managers or control who can read and contribute.
Categories organize articles within a base, but managers and contribute access are defined per knowledge base, so one shared base cannot separate them.
Knowledge subscriptions let users follow relevant articles; they do not create separate managers, categories, or access controls for each team.

questions.question: A user cancels a service catalog request for which procurement has already created purchase orders and transfer orders, none of them received yet. What happens to those orders?

options.text: They are canceled along with the request
They stay open until procurement closes them
They are flagged as backordered items instead
They move to the requested item's tasks

explanation.correct: The docs state: "If a service catalog request is canceled, all associated purchase orders and transfer orders that have not been received are canceled." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/service-catalog/c_RequestingAServiceCatalogItem.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Orders that have not been received do not stay open; the docs say they are canceled when the request is canceled.
Backordered is a check box a fulfiller selects when an item is not in stock; canceling the request cancels the unreceived orders instead.
The docs describe no transfer of orders to tasks; unreceived purchase and transfer orders are canceled with the request.

questions.question: An administrator creates an email notification on the Requested Item table that is sent when a record is updated and approved. Each email must go to the person who opened that requested item. What should be set on the Who will receive tab?

options.text: Users, listing each requester's email address manually
Users/groups in fields, selecting the Opened by field
Subscribable, so requesters can opt in to it
Event parm 1 contains recipient, set to the opener

explanation.correct: Users/groups in fields lets you select fields on the target record that reference users or groups; the system sends the notification to the users in each selected field, so the list varies with each record. The docs' example selects Opened by to notify whoever opened the record. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/t_CreateANotification.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Users field holds a static list of users, so it cannot follow a different opener on each requested item.
Subscribable lets all users subscribe to the notification; it does not address it to each record's opener.
Event parm 1 contains recipient is visible only when Send when is set to Event is fired; this notification is sent on record updates.

questions.question: A team wants to move a heavily used platform application into a portal built with Service Portal. According to the docs, what should they keep in mind before making a large investment?

options.text: Some platform features don't extend to portals
Service Portal must first be activated as a plugin
Any portal change needs the Widget Editor tool
Custom widgets must be built in Workflow Studio

explanation.correct: Service Portal is an alternative presentation layer for the platform, so "not all features of the platform are extended to Service Portal"; the docs advise considering the full application and the abilities of Service Portal before making considerable investments. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-user-interface/service-portal/exploring-service-portal.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Service Portal is a ServiceNow AI Platform feature that is active by default.
Less technical users can make basic configuration changes with Branding Editor and other components; the Widget Editor is the tool for expert users writing scripts.
Custom widgets are developed using AngularJS, Bootstrap, and the ServiceNow API, not in Workflow Studio.
